To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
spatial organization and material items in HIV services can increase the risk of People living with HIV (PLWH) being identified and thus stigmatized.
spatial dimensions of stigma are a feature of HIV care in health facilities in Zambia, South Africa, and other countries.
the spatial organization of HIV services in clinics in Zambia and South African is associated with stigma and that this stigma is experienced by people living with HIV.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways in which spatial organisation and associated items in health facilities influence stigma and HIV treatment.
the spatial organisation of HIV treatment services in government clinics in Zambia and South Africa, and how this is linked to the stigma of HIV.
the relationship between spatial organisation and stigma.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
spatial dimensions of stigma are an important factor for accessing HIV treatment in the clinics.
the spatial dimensions of HIV‐friendly health facility organisation, labelling, and client flow are important in the reduction of HIV stigma.
the study has demonstrated that the spatial organisation of health facilities and the associated material items can contribute to stigma in the context of HIV services.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
stigma is a social process, and that the spatial organisation of health facilities can be a source of stigma, and that stigma can be reduced through thoughtful spatial organisation.
stigma reduction is a complex process that requires multiple approaches and that health facility spatial organisation is one such approach that can be used to reduce HIV stigma.
the spatial organisation of health services and the associated items and labelling of services, spaces and people are linked to the risk of PLHIV “being seen”.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the physical organisation of health services, including spatial demarcation of HIV services and the use of distinctive client flow and material items signifiying HIV‐status, is associated with the risk of PLHIV ‘being seen’ by others.

health workers in Zambia and South African government clinics are concerned that the physical organisation of health facility space may contribute to HIV stigma and that they have devised strategies to reduce this risk, which may be applicable to other contexts.
spatial and material dimensions of stigma need to be recognised and addressed to reduce the social risk of unwanted HIV disclosure and improve the privacy and dignity of health services.
